title: Diversity Curves for Graph Representation Learning
claim: Coarsen graphs step by step, track a structural diversity measure at each size, and use the resulting curves to compare graphs.
layout: 4 stages, left-to-right, dashed arrows linking graphs, curves and scatter
description: A left-to-right pipeline across four stages. At far left, three example graphs are stacked and color-coded: G_A in green (a path-like graph), G_B in blue (a medium-density graph), G_C in dark red (a dense, near-complete graph). Each graph has a gray box to its right showing three progressively smaller coarsened versions, with a 'coarsening' arrow below. Dashed colored arrows lead from each box to a line plot titled Div(G). Its x-axis is graph size |G| from 6 down to 1, and its y-axis is diversity. It shows three colored curves, labeled 'diversity curves', that converge at size 1. A curved dashed arrow labeled 'downstream tasks' leads to a boxed scatter plot labeled 'graph comparisons', where G_A, G_B and G_C appear as separated colored points. Color coding keeps each graph's identity consistent throughout.
caption: Diversity curves for three example graphs. Our framework first coarsens the initial graphs via iterative edge contractions and tracks structural invariants across the coarsening process. Specifically, we compute structural diversity based on a choice of metric on the graph, e.g.\ shortest-path distances. Diversity curves then represent the structural diversity of a graph as a function of the number of nodes in the coarsened graph. The resulting vector representations compare the coarsened geometry of graphs for unsupervised visualisation, clustering, classification, or explanatory tasks.
abstract: Graph-level representations are crucial tools for characterising structural differences between graphs. However, comparing graphs with different cardinalities, even when sampled from the same underlying distribution, remains challenging. Unsupervised tasks in particular require interpretable, scalable, and reliable size-aware graph representations. Our work addresses these issues by tracking the structural diversity of a graph across coarsening levels. The resulting graph embeddings, which we denote diversity curves, are interpretable by construction, efficient, and directly comparable across coarsening hierarchies. Specifically, we track the spread of graphs, a novel isometry invariant that is inherently well-suited for encoding the metric diversity and geometry of graphs. We utilise edge contraction coarsening and prove that this improves expressivity, thus leading to more powerful graph-level representations than structural descriptors alone. Demonstrating their utility over a range of baseline methods in practice, we use diversity curves to (i) cluster and visualise simulated graphs across varying sizes, (ii) distinguish the geometry of single-cell graphs, (iii) compare the structure of molecular graph datasets, and (iv) characterise geometric shapes.
